title: SERL-SQL: Selective Hindsight Distillation for Text-to-SQL Reinforcement Agentic Learning

paper.title: SERL-SQL: Selective Hindsight Distillation for Text-to-SQL Reinforcement Agentic Learning
paper.abstract: Abstract Recent Text-to-SQL systems increasingly rely on multi-turn interaction, execution feedback, and reinforcement learning. However, most existing methods use execution correctness only as a trajectory-level reward, which provides limited guidance for identifying the SQL decisions responsible for success or failure. We propose SERL-SQL , a selective execution-grounded reinforcement learning framework for multi-turn Text-to-SQL agents. SERL-SQL samples on-policy SQL interaction trajectories and uses a training-only teacher to re-score student actions with execution feedback. The resulting teacher–student likelihood gap is converted into bounded, masked weights that reweight GRPO advantages only on SQL and tool-action tokens. In this way, task rewards preserve the optimization direction, while execution hindsight provides localized credit assignment. Experiments on BIRD, Spider, and cross-domain benchmarks show that SERL-SQL achieves competitive performance, reaching 76.56% execution accuracy on BIRD-Dev and 89.92% on Spider-Test. Moreover, our reward-based selection strategy closely approaches the oracle Best-of-N upper bound and consistently outperforms consistency-based selection, showing that SERL-SQL produces high-quality candidates that can be reliably identified by lightweight execution-grounded rewards.

Recent Text-to-SQL research has increasingly shifted from in-context learning ( Wang et al. 2023 ; Gao et al. 2024b ; Pourreza and Rafiei 2023 ; Gao et al. 2024a ) generation to agentic database interaction. Instead of producing a single query directly, modern SQL agents ( Pourreza et al. 2024 ; Talaei et al. 2024 ; Li et al. 2025a ) decompose the process into schema grounding, SQL generation, execution, verification, revision, and selection, enabling models to use database feedback throughout the reasoning process. Representative systems such as Agentar-Scale-SQL ( Wang et al. 2025 ) , Arctic-Text2SQL-R1 ( Yao et al. 2026 ) and MARS-SQL ( Yang et al. 2025 ) further demonstrate the effectiveness of scaling agentic interaction and reinforcement learning for robust Text-to-SQL performance. These advances suggest that realistic Text-to-SQL is no longer merely a sequence generation problem, but an interactive decision-making process grounded in execution. Figure 1: SERL-SQL uses execution hindsight to convert coarse trajectory-level GRPO rewards into selective, reward-aligned credit reweighting for SQL action tokens. Existing agentic Text-to-SQL systems have explored several ways to improve SQL generation through execution-aware training. Search-based and progressive RL methods improve candidate exploration or reward shaping during policy optimization ( Ma et al. 2025 ; Zhang et al. 2026 ) , while SQL-Trail ( Hua et al. 2026 ) use interleaved execution feedback to guide iterative refinement and trajectory evaluation. But they lack real interaction with database, further many works ( Guo et al. 2026 ; Dai et al. 2026b ; Hua et al. 2026 ; Li et al. 2026b ) exploit database feedback for correction, validation, or candidate selection. And FineStep ( Dai et al. 2026a ) show the importance of credit assignment by moving toward finer supervision by assigning credit at the step level for tool-integrated Text-to-SQL. However, these coarse signals cannot localize the SQL decisions responsible for errors, causing credit to diffuse beyond the executable actions that determine correctness. Our key insight is to use execution feedback not only as an outcome reward, but also as training-time hindsight for selective credit assignment. Execution errors, empty results, or incorrect outputs provide privileged evidence about which SQL decisions may be responsible for failure. Instead of exposing such information to the deployed policy or distilling it uniformly, SERL-SQL uses a synchronized teacher to re-score the student’s on-policy actions under the hindsight context. The resulting teacher–student log-probability gap is converted into a bounded GRPO reweighting factor ( Shao et al. 2024 ) , applied only to SQL-relevant and tool-action tokens through a selective action mask. Thus, task rewards preserve the optimization direction, while execution hindsight controls the locality and strength of updates. At inference time, the teacher is removed, and the learned policy operates as a standalone SQL agent. We evaluate SERL-SQL on BIRD, a realistic large-scale database-grounded Text-to-SQL benchmark ( Li et al. 2023 ) . Our current best model achieves 76.56% execution accuracy with reward-based selection over sampled trajectories, closely approaching the oracle best-of- N N result of 77.84%. This small gap suggests that SERL-SQL learns policies whose successful trajectories can be identified by lightweight execution-grounded signals. In summary, our contributions are as follows: • We formulate execution-grounded on-policy distillation for Text-to-SQL, where database feedback is used as teacher-side privileged context to produce bounded, selective advantage reweighting over SQL-relevant and tool-action-relevant tokens. • We validate SERL-SQL on BIRD and Spider, where it achieves 76.56% execution accuracy on BIRD-Dev and 89.92% on Spider-Test. Moreover, reward-based selection closely approaches the oracle Best-of-N upper bound and outperforms consistency-based selection, indicating that SERL-SQL produces high-quality candidates identifiable by execution-grounded rewards. Figure 2: Overview of the SERL-SQL pipeline. (1) schema grounding; (2) multi-turn SQL agent rollout with hierarchical reward verification; (3) selective execution-hindsight re-scoring; and (4) hindsight-guided advantage reweighting. Preliminaries Problem Formulation Given a natural language question q q , a database schema S S , and optional external knowledge e e ( Shi et al. 2025 ; Liu et al. 2025 ) , the agent generates an executable SQL query y y whose result should match the gold answer. We formulate Text-to-SQL as a multi-turn interaction process. At turn t t , the policy observes state s t s_{t} , produces action a t a_{t} , and receives database observation o t o_{t} . A trajectory is defined as τ = ( s 0 , a 0 , o 0 , … , s T , a T , o T ) . \tau=(s_{0},a_{0},o_{0},\ldots,s_{T},a_{T},o_{T}). (1) The final SQL is extracted as y = Etsql ⁡ ( τ ) y=\mathrm{Etsql}(\tau) and evaluated by execution accuracy ( Hong et al. 2025 ) . For N N trajectories sampled from the current policy π θ \pi_{\theta} , the environment returns trajectory-level rewards R n n = 1 N {R^{n}}_{n=1}^{N} based on execution correctness. (5) Although this objective provides a stable reward-aligned update direction, its credit assignment remains coarse: decisive SQL actions, reasoning tokens, and formatting tokens receive the same trajectory-level advantage. On-Policy Distillation On-policy distillation ( Agarwal et al. 2024 ; Zhao et al. 2026 ) provides a complementary token-level training signal. A teacher policy π T \pi_{T} evaluates trajectories sampled from the current student policy and supplies dense supervision: ℒ OPD = ∑ t , i KL [ π T ( ⋅ ∣ h t , y t , < i , c t ex ) ∥ π θ ( ⋅ ∣ h t , y t , < i ) ] , \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{OPD}}=\sum_{t,i}\mathrm{KL}\!\left[\pi_{T}\!\left(\cdot\mid h_{t},y_{t,<i},c_{t}^{\mathrm{ex}}\right)\,\middle\|\,\pi_{\theta}\!\left(\cdot\mid h_{t},y_{t,<i}\right)\right], (6) where c t ex c_{t}^{\mathrm{ex}} denotes teacher-only execution hindsight, such as query results, runtime errors, parser errors, or empty outputs. Directly imitating such a hindsight-conditioned teacher may introduce information leakage, teacher bias, and optimization instability. SERL-SQL therefore uses this signal only for bounded, selective credit reweighting over SQL and tool-action tokens. Methodology SERL-SQL consists of four stages, as shown in Figure 2 . It first grounds the full schema into a compact database context, then samples multi-turn SQL trajectories through iterative generation, execution, and revision. A training-only teacher re-scores the student’s on-policy actions with execution hindsight, and the resulting teacher–student likelihood gap is used to selectively reweight GRPO advantages over executable action tokens. After training, the teacher is removed and the student policy is deployed independently. Schema Grounding Given a natural language question q q and a database schema S S , the schema grounding agent identifies a compact schema subset S ′ ⊆ S S^{\prime}\subseteq S containing the tables, columns, and database values required to answer the question. As illustrated in Figure 2 , the grounding process consists of offline value indexing, question-aware value retrieval, and hybrid schema linking. Let S = { ( T j , C j ) } j = 1 M S=\{(T_{j},C_{j})\}_{j=1}^{M} denote the full schema, where T j T_{j} is a table and C j C_{j} is its set of columns.
